group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 47-year-old man who works as an automotive paint technician and lives with his spouse in a single-story suburban home presented to the emergency department late this afternoon complaining of three days of a progressively wetter cough that began after he helped unload a delivery truck in drizzling weather; over the past 24 hours he has noted intermittent rigors, subjective fever, and increasing shortness of breath when walking from the garage to the kitchen, a distance he usually covers without effort. He purposefully skipped his morning maintenance medications so that “nothing would mask the numbers” and did not use the rescue albuterol inhaler prescribed years ago for episodic wheeze. His medical background is notable for biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy diagnosed in his early thirties that has left him with a chronically reduced glomerular filtration rate in the mid-40 mL/min range—baseline serum creatinine runs 1.6–1.8 mg/dL—and for chronic liver inflammation attributed to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis with early bridging fibrosis on a transient elastography performed last winter; he has never developed ascites, variceal bleeding, or encephalopathy and remains under annual hepatology surveillance. There is no history of stroke, malignancy, decompensated pump function, or residence in an extended-care facility. Routine medications, all omitted this morning, include losartan 50 mg daily, low-dose furosemide every other day for lower-extremity edema control, vitamin D, and ursodiol. He quit a 10-pack-year cigarette habit five years ago, drinks only at holiday gatherings, and denies recreational drug use. Immunizations are current according to the state registry, including both pneumococcal formulations and this season’s influenza shot. Transportation was by his own vehicle; no supplemental oxygen, antipyretics, antibiotics, or intravenous fluids were taken en route. On arrival he was seated upright on the stretcher, speaking in full sentences though pausing for breath between phrases, and fully oriented to person, place, date, and circumstances. Skin was warm and lightly diaphoretic; sclerae were anicteric; conjunctival pallor was absent. Untreated triage vital signs on ambient air at this sea-level facility were: oral temperature 38.1 °C, regular pulse 98 beats per minute confirmed on a three-lead monitor, non-invasive blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg verified manually, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute with mild intercostal effort, and fingertip pulse oximetry fluctuating between 91 % and 92 %. Jugular venous contour was not elevated, and there was no pedal edema. Cardiac examination revealed a steady rhythm without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Pulmonary auscultation demonstrated late inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the posterior left lower lung field; percussion remained resonant throughout, and no dull “stony” note or egophony was appreciated at either base. The abdomen was soft with a palpable but nontender liver edge 2 cm below the right costal margin and no splenomegaly; shifting dullness was absent. A brief neurologic screen showed equal reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, fluent speech, and 5/5 strength in all extremities. Capillary glucose measured immediately before phlebotomy was 108 mg/dL. Peripheral venous blood and a right radial arterial sample were drawn within ten minutes of bay entry prior to any saline flushes, oxygen supplementation, or medication. Basic metabolic panel returned sodium 138 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, chloride 103 mEq/L, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 22 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, consistent with his chronic renal baseline. Complete blood count demonstrated leukocytosis to 13.8 × 10⁹/L with 86 % neutrophils, hematocrit 42 %, hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, and platelets 235 × 10⁹/L. An arterial blood gas obtained while the patient breathed room air revealed pH 7.36, PaCO₂ 35 mm Hg, PaO₂ 69 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 19 mEq/L, reflecting mild hypoxemia with near-physiologic acid-base status. Serum lactate was 1.5 mmol/L. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph performed before any therapy showed a segmental consolidation in the left lower lobe with air bronchograms, clear costophrenic angles, and no layering fluid or meniscus; cardiac silhouette and mediastinal contours were unremarkable. Bedside ultrasound corroborated the absence of anechoic pleural collections. Twelve-lead electrocardiography displayed normal sinus rhythm at 97 beats per minute with preserved intervals and no ischemic changes compared with a tracing from his nephrology clinic six months earlier. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, an induced sputum specimen for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila, and a multiplex respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched prior to antimicrobial initiation. To the moment of this documentation he has received only minimal heparinized saline to maintain a single 18-gauge peripheral catheter and remains on 21 % inspired oxygen, so every physiologic observation, laboratory value, and imaging finding described above represents his untreated presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) uses demographics, comorbidities, examination findings, and initial laboratory and radiographic findings.
1. Demographics: a man's age in years is his base score: 47 points. He lives at home, so no nursing-home points (+0).
2. Comorbidities: chronic liver disease from NASH with fibrosis (+20) and chronic renal disease from IgA nephropathy (+10). No malignancy, heart failure, or cerebrovascular disease (+0 each).
3. Examination: fully oriented, respiratory rate 24 (<30/min), systolic BP 118 (not <90 mmHg), temperature 38.1 °C (neither <35 nor ≥40), and pulse 98 (<125/min): +0 each.
4. Tests: arterial pH 7.36 (not <7.35), BUN 22 (<30 mg/dL), sodium 138 (not <130 mEq/L), glucose 108 (<250 mg/dL), and hematocrit 42% (not <30%): +0 each. Room-air PaO₂ 69 mmHg and saturation 91–92% do not meet the hypoxemia threshold (PaO₂ <60 or saturation <90%): +0. No pleural effusion: +0.
Total = 47 + 20 + 10 = 77 (risk class III).
Final answer: 77
